title: The breastplate
hook: I bind unto myself today the strong name of the Trinity
tomorrow: so many saints and poets. which voice stays with you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, in Patrick's Confession, he told his story the humble way round: I, Patrick, a sinner. Today the week closes with a prayer tradition ties to his name.
screen: `I, PATRICK, A SINNER.` → `A PRAYER IN HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: Jacket, keys, phone, earbuds: the gear that goes on before the door. An old Irish prayer is put on like that. “I bind unto myself today the strong Name of the Trinity.” Some people sing it as a hymn; some pray it while getting dressed. Tradition ties it to Patrick and calls it his breastplate, a prayer worn like armor. So what is armor like that guarding?
screen: `THE GEAR BEFORE THE DOOR.` → `A PRAYER WORN LIKE ARMOR.` → `WHAT IS IT GUARDING?`

segments.voice: Its old name is the Lorica, Latin for breastplate, and the picture is older than Ireland. Paul tells the Thessalonians to put on “the breastplate of faith and love.” The prayer surrounds the wearer: Christ with me, before me, behind me, in me, beneath me, above me. Then it turns outward. Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me. Christ in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me. Christ in every eye that sees me. That's the surprise: the armor doesn't only keep harm out. It changes how the wearer sees everyone else, even the face they're dreading. Now hold the week up. A young nun carried up in a lift. Love at the heart of the body. A peaceful spirit that reaches thousands. Thanks before everything. A morning fire with the foe on its guest list. A sinner's honest story. And today, Christ in every face.
screen: `LORICA: THE BREASTPLATE.` · `CHRIST ON EVERY SIDE.` · `THEN IT TURNS OUTWARD.` · `A WEEK OF SMALL VOICES.` · then, large: `CHRIST IN EVERY EYE.`

segments.voice: Bring three faces to mind that you'll see soon: one easy, one hard, one a stranger. Over each, say the line quietly out loud, Christ in every eye that sees me, or simply say the person's name with a wish for their good. Let the hard face stay a little longer than the others.
The breastplate. The prayer tradition gives to Patrick, worn like armor, asking for Christ on every side and in every face.
One more line for the week: Christ in every eye. Armor that changes how you see. Another week, done.

screen: `DAY 1680 COUNTS.` → `SAINTS AND TEACHERS IN THEIR OWN WORDS · 79 OF 80.` → `TOMORROW: WHICH VOICE STAYS WITH YOU?`

howItsDone: Some Christians pray Saint Patrick's Breastplate in the morning, and the hymn version, I bind unto myself today, is sung in some churches.

it turns outward too: Christ in every eye that sees me.
Paul writes of a breastplate of faith and love
to the Thessalonians. the Irish prayer takes up the same picture.
the breastplate prayer appears in Patrick's Confession

fork.setup: your mom prays Saint Patrick's Breastplate before a meeting with a coworker she can't stand. which part might surprise her?
options: asking God to keep that coworker out of her way all day.
asking for Christ in the eyes of the very people she'll face.
a promise that the meeting will go the way she wants.
fork.reveal: the prayer surrounds the wearer, then turns outward: Christ in every eye that sees me, the hard faces included.

original.note: Latin for breastplate, the prayer's old name.

trapdoor: what you thought: an armor prayer for protection.
what it means: Christ on every side of the wearer, and in every face the wearer meets.
what a scholar hears: the Latin lorica, Paul's breastplate of faith and love, and a prayer tied to Patrick by tradition, not found in his Confession.
guess: an old prayer worn like armor, asking for Christ in every face
the armor an Irish king wore into battle against raiders
the vestment a priest wears over the chest during Mass

Good. The breastplate is for keeping people like Kayla out of your head.

chat.meaning: The breastplate asks for Christ around you and in every face you meet. It guards you, and it changes how you see the person next to you.

Lorica.meaning: Latin: breastplate, the prayer's old name

Trinity.meaning: Father, Son and Holy Spirit: one God, in Christian belief

Thessalonians.meaning: Paul's letters to the church in Thessalonica

The attribution to Patrick is given as tradition; the Breastplate is not in his Confession (see day 1023). The opening line is quoted from C. F. Alexander's hymn version; confirm the wording and capitalization ('the strong Name of the Trinity').

The outward-facing lines (Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, in the mouth of everyone who speaks of me, in every eye that sees me) are paraphrased from the older English translations. Confirm.

Days 1023 and 1149 used the 'Christ on every side' stanza; this lesson names it in one line and spends its time on the outward turn. The Ephesians breastplate from the earlier draft was cut for length.
